title: ChatGPT as a PM.
author: Upstairs_Weird_760
selftext:
I’ve been using AI pretty heavily for my game, but not really in the “tell it what to make and hope for the best” way.

I have a **14–16 week plan for the vertical slice**, broken down by week. Movement, combat, AI, attunements, level building, art, VFX, audio, UI, polish, testing, bug fixing, etc.

A big reason for that is because I know how I am. I’ll think of some cool shit and suddenly want to spend 2 days building it even though it has nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be working on.

So I basically use **ChatGPT as a PM**.

I tell it what I finished, what broke, what feels like shit, and whatever new idea I just came up with. It keeps me focused on the current week, tells me when something is scope creep, and throws stuff into the backlog when it doesn’t need to be worked on yet.

I also use it a lot for design. Not just “is this a good idea?” but actually working through how something should function, whether it fits the game, if it overlaps with another mechanic, etc.

Then once I know what I actually want, I have ChatGPT turn it into a very specific prompt for **Codex**.

Codex is basically my dev team.

I’ll give it something like:

“Add this mechanic. Don’t touch these systems. Expose these values. Keep this behavior. Compile it and stop. I’ll test it.”

Then I test everything myself, tell ChatGPT what worked or didn’t, we figure out the next change, and I send the next task to Codex.

So right now it’s basically:

**Me:** design, testing, tuning, art direction, deciding what stays or gets cut  
**ChatGPT:** PM, planning, scope control, design help, prompts  
**Codex:** coding, debugging, integration, compiling

One thing I’ve realized is that being able to make stuff faster makes **scope control even more important**.

Because now instead of just having bad ideas faster, I can actually IMPLEMENT the bad ideas faster too. lol

I’m also not planning on showing the vertical slice publicly, doing a demo, or EA until it’s around **85% there in polish**.

Not 85% of the whole game finished. I mean the part I’m showing needs to actually look and feel like the game. Good VFX, decent audio, proper enemy presentation, coherent art direction, UI, lighting, etc.

I’ll still do private testing before that obviously.

But I really don’t want my first impression to be some rough ass prototype and then have to explain “well imagine this but better.”

That’s probably been the biggest benefit of the whole AI workflow for me so far. Not that it magically makes the game for me, but it gives me a way to actually run the project like I have a tiny team instead of just randomly bouncing between shit.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I’ve found a very similar way of working, but using sub agents. I make it very clear to the primary that I don’t want it making changes directly and that it needs to assign appropriately specced agents to each task. That means I can run the primary at a good thinking level without it getting creative with my code.

I did at one stage run a full “fake” studio with a distinct thread for each role. It worked really nicely but it really burned through tokens. I would work with the designer, hand a spec to the producer who would coordinate the architect and the developer, QA would review and then it would come back to me and the designer for the play test. It was also quite slow but I found that gave me time to think and to appreciate each feature that was added.

replies.author: Upstairs_Weird_760
replies.body: yeah, thats a cool idea. how much more tokens did it burn?

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body: Hard to tell with the way OpenAI keep changing the packages. It made a Plus account impractical on 5.6, I was getting about 90 minutes work out of every 5 hour window if I worked very casually.

replies.author: Upstairs_Weird_760
replies.body: You also don't need to use Astra for everything. I use Sol light for most coding. if I am adding in a new system, I will use Astra on High.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body: I'm finding 6.1 Sol High to be a decent orchestrator and I've had it pull in Astra when I wanted a deeper analysis. I think it tends towards Terra for simple coding.

comments.author: lulzxdxdxd
comments.body: This setup actually sounds way more useful than the typical AI hype, but I'm curious what breaks when ChatGPT gets something wrong about your game state. Like, does it ever lose track of what you said you finished or mix up which systems are supposed to stay untouched, and does that throw off the whole week or just cost you a few minutes to correct

replies.author: Upstairs_Weird_760
replies.body:
It happens, but usually it costs me a few minutes, not a whole week.

ChatGPT will sometimes remember an older version of a mechanic or think something is finished when it isn’t. I catch most of that before it reaches Codex because I’m still the one approving the task and testing the result.

Codex also has an [`AGENTS.md`](http://AGENTS.md) file with project rules like preserving working systems, not refactoring unrelated stuff, and keeping changes scoped.

A typical Codex task is more like:

**Implement Arcane Ricochet**

Add the next attunement, **Arcane Ricochet**, using the existing attunement framework.

# Intended behavior

When Arcane Ricochet is active, a **right-gauntlet projectile may ricochet off world geometry one time**.

On the first valid blocking hit against world/static geometry:

* calculate a reflected travel direction using the impact normal
* continue the same projectile along the reflected direction
* preserve its existing damage behavior
* preserve most or all projectile speed
* mark that projectile as having consumed its one ricochet

After the ricochet has been consumed, the projectile should behave exactly like a normal projectile on its next blocking hit.

# Enemy hits

* Hitting an enemy should still apply normal projectile damage
* Enemy hits should **not** trigger the ricochet
* Do not bounce through or off enemies

# Important edge cases

Avoid the projectile immediately colliding with the same surface again after reflection.

If necessary:

* offset the projectile slightly away from the impact surface before continuing
* preserve the reflected velocity cleanly

Avoid recursive hit events or multiple ricochets from one collision.

# Attunement integration

Use the existing player attunement/component architecture.

Arcane Ricochet should only affect projectiles fired while the player currently owns the attunement.

Prefer a simple projectile-level flag/state rather than repeatedly querying the player after the projectile has spawned.

Do not create a generalized projectile-modifier framework unless the existing architecture already provides an obvious place for this.

# Tuning

Expose only what is useful:

* Ricochet Enabled
* Max Ricochets = 1
* Ricochet Speed Retention, default around `1.0`

Keep the slice behavior at **one bounce**.

# Presentation hook

Add an optional event/hook when a ricochet successfully occurs so we can later spawn a Niagara flash/effect at the impact location.

Do **not** build the VFX yet.

# Logging

Add concise development logging for successful ricochets, for example:

`ArcaneRicochet: Bounce 1 speed=XXXX`

Do not spam logs for normal projectile hits.

# Constraints

* Right-gauntlet projectile only
* One ricochet only
* No enemy bouncing
* No chaining system
* No new projectile types
* No VFX work yet
* Do not change existing projectile damage, recoil, Pawn collision fixes, or player movement

Compile only. I will test manually.

Stop after compile and summarize:

* files changed
* where ricochet eligibility is stored
* how the reflection direction is calculated
* how repeat collisions are prevented
* where the future VFX hook is exposed



Then i push it to Git.

comments.author: JJBareaIsLeFather
comments.body:
I feed all my information into another project and have it build the prompts for me. At some point it's basically the two AI models having a conversation with each other and me feeding the information between them, reading it and making sure it is doing the right thing as a middle man. 

I have documentation that is automatically updated and kept achieved after every change I have it make, and make a separate archive for the files themselves Everytime. For most my projects once I get it to a playable alpha state I have it build me a basic game launcher that also stores all the previous versions of the game.
